Latent Lattice Language Models

Shivam Duggal ††thanks: Work done during summer internship at Adobe. Affiliation: MIT CSAIL Affiliation: Adobe    Zongze Wu Affiliation: Adobe    William T. Freeman Affiliation: MIT CSAIL    Antonio Torralba Affiliation: MIT CSAIL    Richard Zhang   Eli Shechtman Affiliation: Adobe
Abstract

Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer–SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream’s attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.4115.41 to 14.4014.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.4115.41 (base Transformer) and 14.2214.22 (Transformer with the same enhancements) to 13.6113.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN–Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN and Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4×4\times larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation. Project Page: https://shivamduggal4.github.io/latent-lattice-language-models/

1 Introduction

Language models accept raw text as input, transform it through internal representations, and predict subsequent text. Like most learned systems, this process relies on some form of latent computation. But what, precisely, is the latent computation in a large language model?

In a standard autoregressive LLM, each token is processed by a stack of layers along a single residual stream, and this one latent does several jobs at once. At every layer, it reads from memory through attention queries, writes to memory through keys and values, updates itself through the MLP, and, at the top, is decoded into the next token. The memory it writes to, the KV cache, is an append-only record that stays fixed once written; the residual stream carries all of the active computation. Recent work increases the computation performed on this stream: deeper or looped layers apply more updates per token Dehghani et al. (2019); Geiping et al. (2025); Zhu et al. (2026), continuous latent reasoning continues latent processing between tokens Hao et al. (2024); Wu et al. (2026); Zeng et al. (2026); Shen et al. (2025), and richer residual connections, such as hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, improve how the stream carries information across depth Zhu et al. (2025); Xie et al. (2026); Team et al. (2026); Zhou et al. (2025).

These approaches give the residual stream more to compute. We focus instead on increasing computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We propose a lattice of computational latents: alongside the vertical latent htℓh_{t}^{\ell} that flows through depth (blue arrows in Fig. 1), each Lattice layer maintains its own horizontal latent rtℓr_{t}^{\ell} (orange arrows), updated recurrently across timesteps. We call this architecture the Lattice of Latents, and a language model built on it the Latent Lattice Language Model (LLLM). Like residual-stream enhancements (Zhu et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2026; Team et al., 2026), the Lattice augments the vertical stream, but rather than widening or rerouting it through depth, it adds companion computational states that persist across tokens. The horizontal latents add fixed-size recurrent state without additional token positions or KV-cache entries. So, how does this horizontal flow of information support the vertical latent?

At each step of computation – layer ℓ\ell, timestep tt – two streams of active information are available: the vertical latent htℓ−1h_{t}^{\ell-1} from the layer below, and the horizontal latent rtℓr_{t}^{\ell}, formed by updating the same layer’s previous state rt−1ℓr_{t-1}^{\ell}. In our Transformer instantiation, both latents jointly drive the layer’s attention and MLP computations. The horizontal latent conditions attention queries and KV-cache writes, modulates the MLP, and, at the topmost Lattice layer, also contributes to output decoding alongside the final vertical latent. We design the horizontal update to be (a) expressive enough to serve as a useful companion to the residual stream, and (b) compatible with token-parallel, teacher-forced training.

Towards these goals, we start with an affine Mamba-style (Gu and Dao, 2024) update in which rtℓr_{t}^{\ell} is updated from rt−1ℓr_{t-1}^{\ell} using the incoming vertical latent htℓ−1h_{t}^{\ell-1}. Conditional on the layer-input sequence, this affine recurrence admits an exact associative scan across token positions. Although the update resembles those in Mamba and hybrid Transformer–SSM models, its role differs. There, the recurrent state acts as a sequence mixer: an internal memory that replaces attention or operates alongside it. Here, attention (or the backbone’s native memory) remains the sequence mixer, and the horizontal latent acts as a companion to the residual stream, conditioning how the vertical stream reads and writes that memory and how its MLP processes it.

In this base update, rt−1ℓ→rtℓr_{t-1}^{\ell}\to r_{t}^{\ell}, the horizontal latent receives new information only through the incoming vertical latent (the residual stream) htℓ−1h_{t}^{\ell-1}. We therefore add three enhancements that enrich the horizontal pathway: input injection feeds the token embedding directly into every layer’s update, so each horizontal latent sees the current token without relying on the vertical stream to preserve it; a nonlinear depth-wise readout stream lets each layer’s readout of its horizontal latent depend on those of the layers below, adding nonlinear cross-layer computation on top of the per-layer affine recurrences; and top-to-bottom feedback feeds the top layer’s horizontal latent into the bottom layer’s update at the next timestep, so the most processed state of the previous token informs the earliest computation on the current one. The first two preserve the parallel scan, keeping our main models single-pass at approximately matched compute. The top-to-bottom feedback does not preserve token parallelism, so we approximate it with a few token-parallel Jacobi passes (Wu et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026), at about 2.6×2.6\times the FLOPs for three passes during training; at inference, the same model can instead be rolled out sequentially at the base FLOPs.

Across pretraining budgets from 10B to 30B FineWeb-Edu tokens, the Lattice of Latents improves language-modeling quality at approximately matched parameters and compute (Tab. 1, Tab. 3, Fig. 7). At 20B tokens, a 406M-parameter LLLM with input injection and the depth-wise readout stream lowers FineWeb-Edu perplexity from 15.4115.41 to 14.4014.40, matching a 1.5×1.5\times larger, 40-layer Transformer. A separately trained LLLM with the nonlinear top-to-bottom refiner, run with three Jacobi sweeps (at higher FLOPs), lowers perplexity further to 14.0314.03 (Tab. 1). These gains extend to out-of-distribution perplexity, downstream tasks, and finetuned mathematical reasoning (GSM8K). As a memory-conditioning residual-stream enhancement, the Lattice alone lowers perplexity more than hyper-connections, mHC, or value residuals, and it composes with them (Sec. 4.2): combined with hyper-connections and input residuals, it reaches 13.6113.61, versus 14.2214.22 without the Lattice (Fig. 3).

The Lattice is not specific to softmax attention. We also instantiate it on Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN–Mamba-2 hybrids, where the horizontal latents condition the backbones’ native memory-read, write, and update operations. After 10B-token pretraining, at approximately matched parameter counts, the Lattice improves perplexity at every native state size we test; Lattice GDN and Lattice Triadic GDN each outperform pure baselines holding 4×4\times as many native-state entries. Downstream gains also hold across GDN, Mamba-2, and GDN–Mamba-2 hybrids: adding the Lattice improves the nine-task average in nearly every comparison, spanning five native-state budgets and both zero- and five-shot settings. Probing GDN’s recurrent memory reveals a structural correlate of these gains: at matched native-state sizes, Lattice models exhibit more concentrated state spectra and greater query alignment with the leading memory direction. These observations are consistent with more effective use of native memory.

Overall, comparisons at similar parameter and compute budgets show that allocating capacity to both vertical and horizontal latents outperforms spending it on residual-stream width or network depth alone in the tested configurations. Together, these results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation.

2 Related Work

More computation on a single stream.

Recent work increases how much computation a language model applies to each token. Along depth, models add layers or repeatedly apply a shared stack (Dehghani et al., 2019; Geiping et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026); along time, continuous latent reasoning feeds the final hidden state back as the next input, running additional latent steps before emitting a token (Hao et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2026), with Jacobi-style refinement recovering token-parallel training (Zeng et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). Both directions apply more updates to one active stream, and often grow persistent memory with it: extra layers and loop-specific caches, or latent thoughts held as extra positions, add KV-cache entries. The Lattice instead increases computational capacity by maintaining one active latent per Lattice layer that persists across tokens, without adding per-token KV-cache entries.

Residual-stream enhancements.

A complementary line of work changes how the residual stream carries information through depth. Hyper-connections expand it into parallel streams with learned mixing (Zhu et al., 2025), which mHC constrains to be doubly stochastic (Xie et al., 2026); attention residuals replace the fixed residual sum with attention over earlier layers’ outputs (Team et al., 2026); value residuals reuse first-layer values in later layers (Zhou et al., 2025); and input residuals re-inject the token embedding before every layer. These methods widen or reroute per-token computation through depth, but none gives a layer its own state that persists from one token to the next. The Lattice adds such states and composes with these enhancements: in our experiments, adding it lowers perplexity on top of standard, input-residual, and hyper-connected residual streams (Sec. 3.3).

Recurrent sequence models and hybrids.

Our affine horizontal update shares the scan-parallel form of linear recurrent models such as Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2024; Dao and Gu, 2024), Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025), and DeltaProduct (Siems et al., 2025), whose transitions remain linear or affine in the previous state. In these models, and in hybrids that replace attention with SSM layers at selected depths (Lieber et al., 2024) or run them alongside attention heads (Dong et al., 2024), the recurrent state is a sequence mixer: it substitutes for or supplements attention as the means of reading the past. In the Lattice, the horizontal latent is instead a companion to the residual stream: in Transformers, softmax attention is retained, and the latent conditions attention, its KV-cache writes, and the MLP. Because this role is distinct from sequence mixing, the Lattice also complements recurrent backbones: on GDN, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN–Mamba-2 hybrids, it lowers perplexity at approximately matched parameter counts (Sec. 3.4).

Recurrence within Transformers.

Other work brings recurrence into Transformers without replacing attention. Mozer et al. (2026a) argue that feedforward Transformers push evolving state into ever-deeper layers, exhausting depth, and call for recurrence. NextLat (Teoh et al., 2025) keeps the architecture unchanged and adds an auxiliary objective that trains a latent dynamics model to predict the next hidden state, encouraging recurrent-like belief states; the Lattice instead adds explicit recurrent states to the architecture. Several concurrent works add recurrent or multi-stream pathways, typically feeding a deeper representation from the previous token back into the current token’s computation (Wang et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Cai et al., 2026; Mozer et al., 2026b), or separating state preparation from next-token prediction into distinct streams (Monea et al., 2026). Among these, T2MLR (Cai et al., 2026) is closest to our Jacobi refiner, though its recurrent object is a cached vertical representation rather than a lattice of layer-wise horizontal states. These works largely add a single feedback pathway or separate two roles, whereas the Lattice maintains a persistent latent at every Lattice layer; Appendix A.1 gives detailed description of concurrent works.

3 Method

We propose the Lattice of Latents, an augmentation that distributes computation across a lattice of latents rather than relying only on the usual single residual-stream latent per token. The latent computation spans two axes. Along the vertical axis (network depth), the per-token latent is initialized from the current token embedding and flows bottom-to-top through the backbone’s layers, where it is updated by attention or recurrent state computations followed by a position-wise MLP, before being decoded into the next-token distribution. Along the horizontal axis (time), the Lattice of Latents adds one persistent latent vector at each layer of an intermediate Lattice block, evolving across timesteps rather than through depth. Each horizontal latent remains at its own layer and abstraction level, assisting the vertical stream by conditioning that layer’s memory reads and updates. In our Transformer instantiation, we additionally study MLP modulation. The Lattice thereby increases computational capacity –– the number of active computational states a model maintains by adding companion states to the residual stream, which condition the computation of the residual stream, rather than simply widening the residual stream or adding residual pathways through depth.

We integrate the Lattice of Latents into standard Transformers, Transformers with residual-stream enhancements (hyper-connections, mHC, value residuals, and input residuals), and recurrent backbones: Gated DeltaNet (GDN), Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN–Mamba-2 hybrids. We begin with background on the per-token computational graph of the vertical latent (Sec. 3.1), then formulate the Lattice of Latents (Sec. 3.2), its composition with residual-stream enhancements (Sec. 3.3), and its extension to recurrent backbones (Sec. 3.4).

3.1 Background: Computation with a Single Active Latent

The per-token computational graph of the vertical latent.

Consider an autoregressive Transformer of depth NN and width dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}}, processing a token stream x1,x2,…x_{1},x_{2},\dots. At timestep tt, the model maps the input token xtx_{t} to a distribution over the next token xt+1x_{t+1} through a single residual-stream latent htℓ∈ℝdmodelh_{t}^{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}}, initialized from the token embedding ht0h_{t}^{0} and refined across the NN layers. Layer ℓ∈{1,…,N}\ell\in\{1,\dots,N\} updates this latent with a pre-norm attention block followed by an MLP block:

qtℓ,ktℓ,vtℓ\displaystyle q_{t}^{\ell},\,k_{t}^{\ell},\,v_{t}^{\ell} =Wqℓ​h^,Wkℓ​h^,Wvℓ​h^\displaystyle=W_{q}^{\ell}\hat{h},\;W_{k}^{\ell}\hat{h},\;W_{v}^{\ell}\hat{h}
h¯tℓ\displaystyle\bar{h}_{t}^{\ell} =htℓ−1+Woℓ​Attn​(qtℓ,ℳtℓ)\displaystyle=h_{t}^{\ell-1}+W_{o}^{\ell}\,\mathrm{Attn}\!\big(q_{t}^{\ell},\mathcal{M}_{t}^{\ell}\big)
htℓ\displaystyle h_{t}^{\ell} =h¯tℓ+MLPℓ​(Norm⁡(h¯tℓ)),\displaystyle=\bar{h}_{t}^{\ell}+\mathrm{MLP}^{\ell}\!\big(\mathrm{Norm}(\bar{h}_{t}^{\ell})\big),

where h^=Norm⁡(htℓ−1)\hat{h}=\mathrm{Norm}(h_{t}^{\ell-1}), Norm\mathrm{Norm} is RMSNorm and ℳtℓ={(ksℓ,vsℓ)}s≤t\mathcal{M}_{t}^{\ell}=\{(k_{s}^{\ell},v_{s}^{\ell})\}_{s\leq t} is the layer-ℓ\ell KV cache to which each token appends its keys and values. The final latent is decoded as p⁡(xt+1∣x≤t)=softmax⁡(WU​Norm​(htN))p(x_{t+1}\mid x_{\leq t})=\mathrm{softmax}\big(W_{U}\,\mathrm{Norm}(h_{t}^{N})\big). Thus one latent per token does all the active computation (reading memory, writing to it, and producing the output), while the KV cache passively stores its past projections.

The recurrent view of the vertical latent.

Continuous latent reasoning (Hao et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2026) extends this pathway across timesteps by feeding the previous step’s final-layer latent back as the next input, ht0=ht−1Nh_{t}^{0}=h_{t-1}^{N}, bypassing decoding and re-embedding. The feedback can thus carry more than the log2⁡V\log_{2}V bits of a discrete token, and the vertical latent becomes a running state across time. A standard Transformer instead re-initializes its vertical latent from the token embedding at every timestep.

3.2 The Lattice of Latents

How can we increase the computational capacity of this single active latent? One could widen it (larger dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}}), replicate it into parallel depth-wise streams as in hyper-connections, or add latents along a different axis. We take the third route: each Lattice layer ℓ\ell maintains its own horizontal latent rtℓr_{t}^{\ell} that runs across timesteps, initialized from a learned state and updated from its previous value rt−1ℓr_{t-1}^{\ell} and the incoming vertical latent htℓ−1h_{t}^{\ell-1}. The vertical latent advances through depth at each timestep and the horizontal latents advance through time at each layer; together they form a lattice. We compare this against widening and show that it composes with residual-stream enhancements. Below we describe how the horizontal latents act (Sec. 3.2.1) and how they are updated (Sec. 3.2.2).

3.2.1 How the horizontal latents act

Let rtℓ∈ℝdrr_{t}^{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{r}} be the horizontal latent at layer ℓ\ell and timestep tt, with width drd_{r} chosen independently of dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}}. A standard Transformer layer computes from the vertical latent htℓ−1h_{t}^{\ell-1} and its KV cache. In the Lattice, layer ℓ\ell has two latent inputs: the vertical latent htℓ−1h_{t}^{\ell-1} from the layer below, and the horizontal latent rtℓr_{t}^{\ell}, updated from the same layer’s previous state rt−1ℓr_{t-1}^{\ell}. Together they condition the layer’s attention and MLP, and thus both the residual update that produces htℓh_{t}^{\ell} and the keys and values written to memory. Optionally, the topmost Lattice layer’s horizontal latent also contributes to decoding. We detail each contribution below (Fig. 4); all our Lattice Transformers modulate both attention and the MLP. All contributions read the normalized latent r^tℓ=Norm⁡(rtℓ)\hat{r}_{t}^{\ell}=\mathrm{Norm}(r_{t}^{\ell}).

Conditioning Attention via FiLM. The horizontal latent r^tℓ\hat{r}_{t}^{\ell} modulates the query, key, and value projections of h^=Norm⁡(htℓ−1)\hat{h}=\mathrm{Norm}(h_{t}^{\ell-1}) via Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) (Perez et al., 2017):

qtℓ\displaystyle q_{t}^{\ell} =(Wqℓ​h^)⊙(1+γq​(r^tℓ))+βq​(r^tℓ)\displaystyle=\big(W_{q}^{\ell}\hat{h}\big)\odot\big(1+\gamma_{q}(\hat{r}_{t}^{\ell})\big)+\beta_{q}(\hat{r}_{t}^{\ell})
γ(⋅)​(r^tℓ)\displaystyle\gamma_{(\cdot)}(\hat{r}_{t}^{\ell}) =tanh⁡(W(⋅)γ​r^tℓ)β(⋅)​(r^tℓ)=W(⋅)β​r^tℓ\displaystyle=\tanh\big(W^{\gamma}_{(\cdot)}\hat{r}_{t}^{\ell}\big)\qquad\beta_{(\cdot)}(\hat{r}_{t}^{\ell})=W^{\beta}_{(\cdot)}\hat{r}_{t}^{\ell}

and likewise for ktℓk_{t}^{\ell} and vtℓv_{t}^{\ell}. The multiplicative gain 1+γ∈(0,2)1+\gamma\in(0,2) is bounded, while β\beta is an additive shift; each of q,k,vq,k,v has its own layer-specific, zero-initialized WγW^{\gamma} and WβW^{\beta}, so the modulation starts as the identity. The gain γ\gamma may be shared across channel groups within each head, while β\beta is always per-channel. Because the modulated ktℓ,vtℓk_{t}^{\ell},v_{t}^{\ell} are written to ℳℓ\mathcal{M}^{\ell}, the horizontal latent shapes both the memory read and the memory write. The attention output, projected by WoℓW_{o}^{\ell}, is added to the vertical latent as before, giving the MLP input h¯tℓ\bar{h}_{t}^{\ell}.

Modulating MLP. The horizontal latent also shifts the gate and up pre-activations of the layer’s SwiGLU MLP, each through its own zero-initialized map:

m\displaystyle m =Norm⁡(h¯tℓ)gate=Wgateℓ​m+βgate​(r^tℓ)\displaystyle=\mathrm{Norm}(\bar{h}_{t}^{\ell})\qquad\mathrm{gate}=W_{\mathrm{gate}}^{\ell}m+\beta_{\mathrm{gate}}(\hat{r}_{t}^{\ell})
up\displaystyle\mathrm{up} =Wupℓ​m+βup​(r^tℓ).\displaystyle=W_{\mathrm{up}}^{\ell}m+\beta_{\mathrm{up}}(\hat{r}_{t}^{\ell}).

MLP output Wdownℓ​(SiLU⁡(gate)⊙up)W_{\mathrm{down}}^{\ell}\big(\mathrm{SiLU}(\mathrm{gate})\odot\mathrm{up}\big) is added to h¯tℓ\bar{h}_{t}^{\ell}, giving htℓh_{t}^{\ell}.

Modulating Decoding. Optionally, the topmost Lattice layer’s normalized horizontal latent and the final vertical latent are projected into a shared readout space, and the next token is decoded from their sum (details in Appendix A.2.1). We use this head only with a highly compressed vertical latent (dmodel=256d_{\mathrm{model}}{=}256) (in Fig. 6), where the standard decoder would otherwise read the output distribution from a 256-dimensional latent alone.

3.2.2 How the horizontal latents are updated

We divide the backbone’s layers into an early block (E), an intermediate Lattice block (L), and a late block (D); horizontal latents exist only in L. For ℓ∈L\ell\in L, the update takes the form:

rtℓ=U⁡(rt−1ℓ,htℓ−1,ht0,rt−1top)r_{t}^{\ell}=U\big(r_{t-1}^{\ell};\;h_{t}^{\ell-1},\;h_{t}^{0},\;r_{t-1}^{\mathrm{top}}\big)

The base update uses the layer’s own history rt−1ℓr_{t-1}^{\ell} and the incoming vertical latent htℓ−1h_{t}^{\ell-1}. Input injection adds the token embedding ht0h_{t}^{0}, and the optional Jacobi refiner adds feedback rt−1topr_{t-1}^{\mathrm{top}} from the top Lattice layer one timestep back, injected only at the bottom Lattice layer and taken from the previous sweep. The depth-wise readout stream (vstream or vs in model labels), which passes information upward from lower horizontal latents within a timestep, enriches each layer’s readout rather than entering UU. We describe each mechanism below (Fig. 5).

Affine update from rt−1ℓr_{t-1}^{\ell} to rtℓr_{t}^{\ell}. To keep training token-parallel and teacher-forced, we need a recurrence that admits an exact associative scan across timesteps rather than a token-by-token loop. An affine transition with input-dependent coefficients has this property. Following linear attention and Mamba-style state-space models, we use one whose coefficients depend only on the current layer input, never directly on the previous horizontal state. The affine update reads a normalized copy of the vertical latent ntℓ=Normin​(htℓ−1)n_{t}^{\ell}=\mathrm{Norm}_{\mathrm{in}}(h_{t}^{\ell-1}), and is defined as:

Δtℓ\displaystyle\Delta_{t}^{\ell} =softplus⁡(WΔℓ​ntℓ+bΔℓ)\displaystyle=\mathrm{softplus}\big(W_{\Delta}^{\ell}n_{t}^{\ell}+b_{\Delta}^{\ell}\big)
gtℓ\displaystyle g_{t}^{\ell} =exp(−exp(aℓ)⊙Δtℓ)\displaystyle=\exp\big(-\exp(a^{\ell})\odot\Delta_{t}^{\ell}\big)
ctℓ\displaystyle c_{t}^{\ell} =SiLU⁡(Wrℓ​ntℓ+brℓ)\displaystyle=\mathrm{SiLU}\big(W_{r}^{\ell}n_{t}^{\ell}+b_{r}^{\ell}\big)
btℓ\displaystyle b_{t}^{\ell} =(1−gtℓ)⊙ctℓ\displaystyle=(1-g_{t}^{\ell})\odot c_{t}^{\ell}
rtℓ\displaystyle r_{t}^{\ell} =gtℓ⊙rt−1ℓ+btℓ.\displaystyle=g_{t}^{\ell}\odot r_{t-1}^{\ell}+b_{t}^{\ell}.

Here r0ℓr_{0}^{\ell} is a learned initial state before the first token x1x_{1}, and aℓa^{\ell} and bΔℓb_{\Delta}^{\ell} are learned per-channel log-decay rates and time-step biases. Because gtℓg_{t}^{\ell} and btℓb_{t}^{\ell} depend on ntℓn_{t}^{\ell} alone, the transition is exactly affine given the layer-input sequence, so the horizontal states at all token positions are computed with a parallel scan during training. Layers are still evaluated in depth order, each scanning the vertical inputs produced by the layer below. The readout used downstream is r^tℓ=Norm⁡(rtℓ)\hat{r}_{t}^{\ell}=\mathrm{Norm}(r_{t}^{\ell}). Although the update follows a Mamba-style gated affine recurrence, the horizontal latent plays a different role, a companion to the residual stream rather than a sequence mixer, which we revisit for backbones that already maintain recurrent memory (Sec. 3.4).

We call this configuration the base update and label the corresponding models 𝐋𝐋𝐋𝐌⁡(dmodel,dr)\mathbf{LLLM}(d_{\mathrm{model}},d_{r}), with vertical width dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}} and horizontal width drd_{r}; additional mechanisms are marked separately in model labels. The base update can integrate history across time, but on its own it applies no learned nonlinear transformation to its previous state. We therefore study three complementary mechanisms: input injection (inj) and the depth-wise readout stream (vs) add expressivity within a timestep while preserving the parallel scan, whereas the Jacobi refiner adds a nonlinear top-to-bottom feedback pathway across timesteps at the cost of the single-pass guarantee.

Adding the input embedding to the horizontal latent. The base update sees the current input only through htℓ−1h_{t}^{\ell-1}, which by layer ℓ\ell may have discarded information about the raw token identity (see the narrow-vertical-latent ablation, Fig. 6). Input injection (inj) also feeds the normalized token embedding ht0h_{t}^{0} into Δtℓ\Delta_{t}^{\ell} and ctℓc_{t}^{\ell} through zero-initialized projections. These coefficients still depend only on current-timestep inputs, so the transition remains exactly affine and the same parallel scan applies (more details in Appendix A.2.2).

Enhancing layer-wise nonlinearity of the horizontal latent. At layer ℓ\ell, the readout r^tℓ\hat{r}_{t}^{\ell} from the base update and input injection receives information from lower Lattice layers’ horizontal latents only indirectly, through whatever survives in the vertical latent. The depth-wise readout stream (vstream or vs) adds a direct path: a purely depth-wise state stℓ∈ℝdrs_{t}^{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{r}} that runs bottom to top across the Lattice, seeded with stℓ0−1:=0s_{t}^{\ell_{0}-1}:=0 at the first Lattice layer ℓ0\ell_{0}:

stℓ\displaystyle s_{t}^{\ell} =stℓ−1+Ws↑ℓ​SiLU​(Ws↓ℓ​[Norm⁡(r^tℓ),Norm⁡(stℓ−1)]),\displaystyle=s_{t}^{\ell-1}+W_{s\uparrow}^{\ell}\mathrm{SiLU}\Big(W_{s\downarrow}^{\ell}\big[\mathrm{Norm}(\hat{r}_{t}^{\ell}),\,\mathrm{Norm}(s_{t}^{\ell-1})\big]\Big),

where [⋅,⋅][\cdot,\cdot] denotes concatenation. Since Ws↑ℓW_{s\uparrow}^{\ell} is zero-initialized, stℓ≡stℓ−1s_{t}^{\ell}\equiv s_{t}^{\ell-1} at initialization, so with the zero seed the stream is zero throughout the Lattice. The stream carries same-timestep communication across depth, separately from the recurrent update UU, which acts across time. Because stℓs_{t}^{\ell} depends only on same-timestep quantities, it adds a nonlinear dependency across depth but none across time, leaving the base recurrence and its parallel scan untouched. With vs enabled, the enriched readout

r~tℓ:=r^tℓ+Norm⁡(stℓ)\displaystyle\tilde{r}_{t}^{\ell}:=\hat{r}_{t}^{\ell}+\mathrm{Norm}(s_{t}^{\ell})

replaces r^tℓ\hat{r}_{t}^{\ell} wherever it conditions attention or the MLP (Sec. 3.2.1). The state carried across timesteps remains the raw rtℓr_{t}^{\ell}, not r~tℓ\tilde{r}_{t}^{\ell}; the enriched readout influences higher layers’ updates only indirectly, through the vertical stream.

Cross-timestep nonlinear update. Input injection and the depth-wise readout stream use only current-timestep information, so neither feeds a higher layer’s more deeply processed latent back to a lower layer at the next timestep. In the Transformer instantiation, we add this top-to-bottom feedback: the top Lattice layer’s latent at t−1t-1, passed through a zero-initialized SwiGLU, is added to the bottom Lattice layer’s update at tt, making the recurrence nonlinear across timesteps. This feedback is straightforward in a token-by-token rollout but breaks single-pass teacher-forced training, so we approximate it with a Jacobi refiner (Zeng et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026): after an initial pass over the Lattice block, each refinement sweep reruns all Lattice layers in parallel across tokens, taking the feedback from the previous sweep. Unlike Zeng et al. (2026); Wu et al. (2026), which apply Jacobi iteration to the vertical latent (ht0=ht−1Nh_{t}^{0}=h_{t-1}^{N}), we apply it to the horizontal latents. J0 denotes the single-pass model without this cross-timestep feedback and J3 the initial pass followed by two refinement sweeps (≈2.6×\approx 2.6\times the FLOPs). At inference, the feedback can instead be computed exactly by sequential rollout; we evaluate both (details in Appendix A.2.3).

3.3 Composing with Residual-Stream Enhancements

Because the Lattice conditions each block’s computation rather than the residual pathway itself, it combines with residual-stream enhancements without changing the horizontal update. An input residual re-injects the normalized token embedding before every layer, htℓ−1←λrℓ​htℓ−1+λ0ℓ​Norm​(ht0)h_{t}^{\ell-1}\leftarrow\lambda_{r}^{\ell}h_{t}^{\ell-1}+\lambda_{0}^{\ell}\,\mathrm{Norm}(h_{t}^{0}), with learned per-layer scalars; the horizontal update then reads this re-injected layer input as htℓ−1h_{t}^{\ell-1}. This differs from input injection (inj), which feeds the embedding into the horizontal update rather than into the residual stream. Hyper-connections (Zhu et al., 2025) expand the residual stream into nn parallel streams that a learned router mixes into each block’s input and remixes after its output (mHC (Xie et al., 2026) constrains this mixing to be doubly stochastic). With hyper-connections, each Lattice layer’s horizontal update reads the mixed block input in place of htℓ−1h_{t}^{\ell-1}, FiLM conditions that block’s QKV and MLP computations as in Sec. 3.2.1, and the router writes the block outputs back to the streams. A single horizontal latent per Lattice layer is shared across the nn streams. A value residual (Zhou et al., 2025) mixes each layer’s attention values with those of the first layer; in Lattice layers, the mix is applied after FiLM conditioning and before attention. In our experiments, we compare the Lattice against these residual-stream enhancements and evaluate their combinations.

3.4 Lattice of Latents on Recurrent Backbones

Although the horizontal update uses a Mamba-style recurrence, the Lattice also complements backbones that already maintain recurrent memory. We instantiate it on GDN, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN--Mamba-2 hybrids. Unlike a Transformer’s growing KV cache, these backbones keep native memories of fixed size: matrix-valued states per head in GDN and Mamba-2, and a three-dimensional state per head in Triadic GDN, which adds a routing axis. The Lattice leaves these memories intact and adds a separate horizontal latent that conditions how they are used.11 1 We use “state” and “memory” interchangeably for the backbones’ native recurrent memories, which play a role analogous to the KV cache. The horizontal latent is also recurrent state, but its role is to condition the computations driven by the vertical residual stream.

We keep the base update, with input injection and the depth-wise readout stream as options, and apply FiLM to each backbone’s memory read, write, and update quantities: in GDN, Q, K, V, the retention (α\alpha) and update-strength (β\beta) pre-activations, and the output gate; in Mamba-2, the read (C) and write (B) projections, the input stream, the time-step pre-activation, and the output gate. Triadic GDN additionally conditions its routing factors, and GDN–Mamba-2 hybrids follow the settings of each layer’s backbone. All modulation weights are zero-initialized, and modulation is applied before each quantity’s constraining transformation. These comparisons use unmodulated MLPs, the ordinary decoding head, and no Jacobi refiner; further details are in the Appendix.

To separate this from simply enlarging native memory, we compare models with and without the Lattice across native-state budgets at approximately matched parameters. In GDN, for example, a 256-dimensional horizontal latent combined with 65,536 native state entries per layer achieves lower perplexity than a pure GDN with 262,144 entries. We also analyze GDN’s state geometry (spectra, effective and stable rank, and query alignment with the leading memory direction) with and without the Lattice. The distinction is functional: the horizontal latent is itself persistent state, but rather than expanding the backbone’s associative memory, it provides a learned, history-dependent pathway that conditions the vertical stream’s computation. We hypothesize that this added computational capacity helps the model use its native memory more effectively, complementing rather than replicating increases in memory capacity; our experiments are consistent with this hypothesis.

4 Experiments

We evaluate the Lattice of Latents on language modeling and zero- and five-shot downstream tasks for both Transformer and recurrent backbones, and combine it with residual-stream enhancements. We then deconstruct the Lattice into its components and study its effect on GDN’s native memory. Further experiments on – jacobi refiner, comparison with short conv, stateless modulation, downstream evaluations, GSM8K finetuning, and other details are in Appendix Sec. A.3.

4.1 Transformer Backbones

We pretrain 400M–600M-parameter LLLMs and Transformer baselines on FineWeb-Edu for 10B, 20B, or 30B tokens; the larger budgets exceed Chinchilla-style compute-optimal budgets at these sizes. We report held-out perplexity on FineWeb-Edu (in-domain) and on Pile, LAMBADA (OpenAI and Standard), and Nemotron-CC (out-of-domain), and zero- and five-shot accuracy on nine lm-evaluation-harness tasks; evaluation and compute-accounting details are in Appendix Sec. A.3.

Language modeling.

Table 1 compares 400M–600M models pretrained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens. At 400M, LLLM(945,256)(945,256) matches Base-24L in parameters and forward compute (406.5 M / 0.72 vs. 406.7 M / 0.71 GFLOP/token), yet lowers FineWeb-Edu perplexity from 15.4115.41 to 14.5414.54 (−5.6%-5.6\%) and out-of-domain perplexity by 33–11%11\% on every set. Adding input-injection + vstream, with the vertical width reduced from 945945 to 908908 to hold parameters and FLOPs approximately fixed, improves further, most on out-of-domain data (the best Pile perplexity in the table, 24.1024.10). Jacobi refinement gives the strongest 400M results: LLLM-410 J3 attains the best FineWeb-Edu (14.0314.03), LAMBADA, and Nemotron-CC perplexities in the 400M block, but its three sweeps raise estimated forward compute to 1.851.85 GFLOP/token. Exact sequential rollout of the same checkpoint needs only 0.720.72 GFLOP/token but raises FineWeb-Edu perplexity to 14.7314.73. Training with a randomized number of Jacobi iterations, as in PonderLM-2 (Zeng et al., 2026), can remove this gap (Sec. 4.4); we train with three fixed sweeps.

At 600M, LLLM(1024,1024)(1024,1024) achieves the best perplexity on every dataset in its block (FineWeb-Edu 13.7013.70), outperforming both width-scaled Transformers and the depth-scaled Base-40L, which has nearly identical forward compute (1.101.10 GFLOP/token). Thus, at comparable parameters and compute, splitting capacity between vertical and horizontal latents outperforms spending it on residual-stream width or depth alone. The advantage also holds across scales: the 405.6 M input-injection + vstream model matches the 609M Base-40L on FineWeb-Edu (14.4014.40) and beats it on Pile and both LAMBADA variants, trailing only on Nemotron-CC, with 33%33\% fewer parameters and 35%35\% less estimated forward compute. Under three-sweep evaluation, the 407M J3 model surpasses Base-40L on all five datasets, though at higher inference compute. Results at 30B tokens are in Appendix Tab. 3.

Downstream evaluation.

Table 4 reports the nine-task average accuracy (Task Avg.) of the same 20B-token models. At matched 400M scale, LLLM(945,256)(945,256) improves on Base-24L from 45.4645.46 to 47.6747.67 zero-shot (+2.21+2.21 points) and from 46.1946.19 to 47.7947.79 five-shot (+1.60+1.60). Adding input-injection + vstream raises five-shot accuracy further to 48.1648.16, and Jacobi refinement gives the strongest 400M averages, 48.6948.69 zero-shot and 49.3849.38 five-shot (+3.23+3.23 and +3.19+3.19 over Base-24L). At 600M, LLLM(1024,1024)(1024,1024) outperforms Base-40L by 1.171.17 points zero-shot and 2.002.00 five-shot. The 407M J3 model also exceeds Base-40L, by 1.331.33 and 2.012.01 points, with roughly one-third fewer parameters, though its three sweeps require more inference compute. Thus, the perplexity gains carry over to downstream accuracy.

4.2 Composing with Residual-Stream Enhancements

The Lattice adds a horizontal pathway that carries latents across time, whereas recent residual-stream enhancements reshape how information flows vertically, across depth. We test whether the two are complementary by pretraining 400M models on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens with hyper-connections (HC) (Zhu et al., 2025), manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC) (Xie et al., 2026), value residuals (Zhou et al., 2025), and nanochat-style input residuals (x0) (Karpathy, 2025), alone and in combination, with and without the Lattice (Fig. 3); the Lattice models narrow the vertical width from 10241024 to 932932 to remain iso-parameter (details in Appendix Sec. A.4.2). On its own, the Lattice lowers FineWeb-Edu perplexity from 15.4115.41 to 14.4714.47, more than HC (15.2815.28), mHC (14.9314.93), or value residuals (14.6914.69), and is second only to x0 (14.3414.34). More importantly, its gains add to theirs: the Lattice lowers HC from 15.2815.28 to 14.2114.21 (−7.0%-7.0\%) and HC + x0 from 14.2214.22 to 13.6113.61 (−4.3%-4.3\%). Lattice + HC + x0 is the best model overall, 11.7%11.7\% below the plain Transformer and 3.9%3.9\% below the strongest Transformer composition (x0 + value, 14.1614.16). Thus, horizontal latents are not a substitute for a better residual stream; they are an orthogonal axis that compounds with it.

4.3 Recurrent Backbones

We pretrain GDN, Mamba2, Triadic GDN, and GDN–Mamba2 hybrids without sliding-window attention (no-SWA) on 10B FineWeb-Edu tokens, pairing each pure backbone with a Lattice counterpart of the same native-state geometry and approximately matched parameter count (∼\sim405M). We sweep 16K, 32K, 64K, 128K, and 256K native-state entries per mixer (1K =1024=1024 scalar entries), excluding the added horizontal latents and auxiliary convolution states. For GDN, the state size is H​dk​dvHd_{k}d_{v} for HH heads with per-head key and value dimensions dk,dvd_{k},d_{v}; we use (H,dk,dv)=(16,16,64)(H,d_{k},d_{v})=(16,16,64), (16,32,64)(16,32,64), (16,64,64)(16,64,64), (8,128,128)(8,128,128), and (4,256,256)(4,256,256), and vary the other backbones similarly (Appendix). The horizontal latent modulates only the mixer’s memory read, write, and update quantities, not the MLP or decoding. Perplexity results use input-injection + vstream, with the Lattice model’s vertical residual stream (dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}}) narrowed to offset the added parameters, keeping every comparison iso-parameter. For downstream results, at each state budget and shot setting we select, by nine-task average, the best of three couplings—input-injection + vstream and two vstream-only variants that restore the parameter budget by reducing either dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}} or the FFN width (more details in Appendix Sec. A.3).

Language modeling.

On FineWeb-Edu (Fig. 2), the Lattice lowers perplexity at every native-state size: by 1.21.2–2.6%2.6\% for GDN, 0.60.6–2.2%2.2\% for Mamba2, 1.11.1–2.1%2.1\% for Triadic GDN, and 0.30.3–1.0%1.0\% for the GDN–Mamba2 hybrid (15.8515.85 vs. 15.9215.92 at 256K). Lattice models can also outperform pure models with four times as many native-state entries per mixer: 64K Lattice GDN beats 256K pure GDN (16.0516.05 vs. 16.1116.11), and 64K Lattice Triadic GDN beats 256K pure Triadic GDN (15.9815.98 vs. 16.0916.09). These results are consistent with the hypothesis that horizontal latent helps vertical residual stream control memory writes and reads, enabling more effective use of native memory (Sec. 4.4).

Downstream evaluation.

On the same nine-task average (Figs. 12 and 13), the selected Lattice model outperforms its pure counterpart in almost all paired comparisons, spanning three backbones (GDN, Mamba2, and the no-SWA hybrid), five state budgets, and two shot settings. Averaged over state budgets, the gains range from +0.53+0.53 to +0.67+0.67 points zero-shot and +0.76+0.76 to +0.95+0.95 points five-shot across backbones, peaking at +1.50+1.50 (Mamba2, 16K, five-shot), and they persist at the largest budget: at 256K, the Lattice adds +0.86+0.86 and +1.06+1.06 points to GDN. Lattice models can again outperform pure models with larger native states. With 8×8\times fewer native entries per mixer, 32K Lattice GDN surpasses 256K pure GDN in both settings (44.8844.88 vs. 44.4544.45 zero-shot), as does the 32K hybrid over the 256K hybrid, and 16K Lattice Mamba2 over 128K pure Mamba2; with 16×16\times fewer, 16K Lattice GDN still exceeds 256K pure GDN zero-shot (44.5744.57 vs. 44.4544.45).

4.4 Analysis

Deconstructing the Lattice.

In this section, we ask where the gains come from, training all models on 10B FineWeb-Edu tokens & reporting validation perplexity. Narrowing the vertical latent alone is costly: Transformer(512,0)(512,0) reaches 18.8718.87, versus 16.9416.94 for the 406 M, 1024-wide Transformer (Fig. 8). Reinvesting that capacity horizontally more than recovers the loss: LLLM(512,512)(512,512) matches the 406 M Transformer with only 291 M parameters (16.9616.96), and at a matched 406 M, LLLM(945,256)(945,256) reaches 15.6315.63 (−7.7%-7.7\%), or 15.4915.49 (−8.5%-8.5\%) with input-injection + vstream. As shown in Fig. 6, spending 200 M more parameters on Transformer width (15.9815.98) or depth (15.8215.82) still trails this 406 M Lattice model. Fig. 6 also isolates the top-to-bottom Jacobi refiner, which feeds the top Lattice layer’s horizontal latent to the bottom layer at the next token: each J3 model (trained with three sweeps) improves on its base-update counterpart, e.g., from 14.8314.83–14.8914.89 to 14.2914.29–14.4014.40 at ∼\sim600 M, at additional inference compute. Prior work (Zeng et al., 2026) has shown that training with a randomized number of Jacobi iterations removes this additional inference cost, matching the performance of sequential rollout.

Figure 7 examines the mechanisms in the hardest regime, a highly compressed 256-dimensional vertical latent (dmodel=256d_{\mathrm{model}}=256). Here, adding horizontal capacity with the base update alone is not enough: LLLM(256,768)(256,768) reaches 19.5819.58, worse than the 512-wide Transformer (18.8718.87). Jacobi refinement alone reduces this to 18.9518.95. Separately, cumulatively adding input injection (18.5518.55), vstream (17.9617.96), the horizontal decoding head with ds=512d_{s}=512 (17.6217.62), a larger Lattice block (E4/L16/D4 to E1/L20/D1; 17.4217.42), and ds=1024d_{s}=1024 (17.1817.18) closes most of the 2.642.64-perplexity gap, leaving the model 0.240.24 behind the 406.7 M Transformer with 21%21\% fewer parameters. These additions also grow the model from 215.8 M to 320.9 M parameters, so they measure combined gains rather than effects at fixed capacity. LLLM(512,512)(512,512) still does better (16.9616.96 with 291 M parameters): these pathways mitigate but do not remove the cost of an extremely narrow vertical latent, so the split between vertical and horizontal capacity matters; most of our main models keep a wide vertical latent with a smaller horizontal one (dr=256d_{r}=256).

Memory geometry and query alignment.

Finally, we ask how the Lattice changes the way GDN uses its native memory. Each GDN head maintains a memory matrix S∈ℝdk×dvS\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times d_{v}}, written with keys and read with queries, where dkd_{k} and dvd_{v} are the per-head key and value dimensions. Writing S=U​Σ​V⊤S=U\Sigma V^{\top} with singular values σ1≥σ2≥⋯\sigma_{1}\geq\sigma_{2}\geq\cdots and leading left singular vector u1∈ℝdku_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}, we measure how concentrated the memory is, using effective and stable ranks. The entropy effective rank rent=exp(−∑ipilogpi)r_{\mathrm{ent}}=\exp\!\big(-\sum_{i}p_{i}\log p_{i}\big), with pi=σi/∑jσjp_{i}=\sigma_{i}/\sum_{j}\sigma_{j}, is the effective number of directions the spectrum spreads over; the stable rank rstable=‖S‖F2/σ12=∑iσi2/σ12r_{\mathrm{stable}}=\|S\|_{F}^{2}/\sigma_{1}^{2}=\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}^{2}/\sigma_{1}^{2} measures how strongly the leading direction dominates. Both lie in [1,min⁡(dk,dv)][1,\min(d_{k},d_{v})]; lower values mean a more concentrated spectrum, but do not by themselves imply less stored information. We also measure the query alignment gain G1=dk​(u1⊤​q)2/‖q‖22G_{1}=d_{k}\,(u_{1}^{\top}q)^{2}/\|q\|_{2}^{2}: the squared cosine between the normalized query q∈ℝdkq\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}} used for reading and u1u_{1}, scaled by dkd_{k} so that an isotropic random query gives 𝔼⁡[G1]=1\mathbb{E}[G_{1}]=1.

Table 2 shows a consistent pattern at every state budget: the Lattice lowers rentr_{\mathrm{ent}} by 9.69.6–18.3%18.3\% and rstabler_{\mathrm{stable}} by 10.910.9–15.0%15.0\%, while raising G1G_{1} by 33.533.5–67.4%67.4\%. The alignment gap widens with state size, from +1.89+1.89 at 16K to +5.36+5.36 at 256K, where Lattice queries align with the leading memory direction 13.3×13.3\times more than chance, versus 8.0×8.0\times for the pure model. Thus, with Lattice, GDN writes a more concentrated memory and reads more strongly along its dominant direction, consistent with the hypothesis that the horizontal latent helps the vertical stream control memory writes and reads.

5 Conclusion

We introduced the Lattice of Latents, which distributes computational capacity across the vertical residual stream and persistent, layer-wise horizontal latents. Rather than replacing sequence memory, these latents act as companion computational states that steer the backbone’s computation. We use an affine horizontal update and introduce enhancements that increase latent expressivity while preserving token-parallel teacher-forced computation within each pass. LLLMs improve language modeling and downstream task averages across Transformer and recurrent backbones. The Lattice also composes with residual-stream enhancements: combined with hyper-connections and input residuals, it outperforms every Transformer variant we test. On recurrent backbones, gains arise at matched native-state sizes and approximately matched parameter counts, with Lattice GDN and Lattice Triadic GDN outperforming pure baselines that use 4×4\times as many native-state entries. Overall, our results suggest that distributing active computational capacity across interacting latents is a promising complement to scaling width, depth, memory, or the residual stream alone.
