Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Extended Related Work

More computation on a single stream.

Extra computation along depth or time often comes with extra persistent memory. In depth-based methods, each added layer brings its own KV cache, and looped models may keep iteration-specific caches, although recent work shares or compresses state across loops (Vendrell et al., 2026; Neill and Reid, 2026). Among continuous latent reasoning methods, Coconut feeds the final hidden state back as the next input, CODI distills such reasoning from an explicit chain-of-thought teacher, and PonderLM-2 brings it into pretraining (Hao et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2026); when latent thoughts are held as extra positions, they also add KV-cache entries. Because consecutive thoughts depend on each other, single-pass teacher forcing no longer applies; PonderLM-2 and PCCoT recover token parallelism with Jacobi-style refinement (Zeng et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026), which inspires our optional Jacobi refiner (App. A.2.3).

Residual-stream enhancements.

We detail three residual-stream enhancements: input residuals, value residuals, and hyper-connections. An input residual re-injects the normalized token embedding before every layer, htℓ−1←λrℓ​htℓ−1+λ0ℓ​Norm​(ht0)h_{t}^{\ell-1}\leftarrow\lambda_{r}^{\ell}h_{t}^{\ell-1}+\lambda_{0}^{\ell}\,\mathrm{Norm}(h_{t}^{0}), with learned per-layer scalars λrℓ,λ0ℓ\lambda_{r}^{\ell},\lambda_{0}^{\ell}. Value residual learning (Zhou et al., 2025) adds a similar shortcut inside attention: each layer mixes its attention values with those of the first layer, vtℓ←λ1ℓ​vt1+λ2ℓ​vtℓv_{t}^{\ell}\leftarrow\lambda_{1}^{\ell}v_{t}^{1}+\lambda_{2}^{\ell}v_{t}^{\ell}, with learned per-layer scalars, so later layers retain direct access to early token information. Hyper-connections (Zhu et al., 2025) expand the residual stream into nn parallel streams: each block reads a learned, input-dependent mixture of the streams, and its output is written back as the streams are remixed; mHC (Xie et al., 2026) constrains this mixing to be doubly stochastic. All three act within a timestep, so they compose directly with the Lattice (Sec. 3.3); the horizontal update reads whatever input the residual design produces. With hyper-connections one horizontal latent per layer is shared across the nn streams.

Recurrent sequence models.

Beyond Mamba-2’s gated recurrence, Gated DeltaNet adds delta-rule state updates, and DeltaProduct composes several Householder-style corrections into a more expressive but still linear transition (Yang et al., 2025; Siems et al., 2025). Work on nonlinear recurrences is complementary: ParaRNN parallelizes general nonlinear recurrences with Newton iterations, and M2RNNs combine nonlinear updates with matrix-valued states (Danieli et al., 2025; Mishra et al., 2026). We keep the temporal update affine, add expressivity through its inputs and readouts, and obtain nonlinear feedback across time only through optional Jacobi refinement. Advances in parallelizable nonlinear recurrences could further strengthen the horizontal latent as a temporal companion to the residual stream.

Recurrence within Transformers (concurrent work).

Full-Bandwidth Transformer (Wang et al., 2026) feeds the previous token’s top-layer state back alongside the next embedding; Latent Recurrent Transformer (Huang et al., 2026) reuses a selected high-level representation as recurrent memory; and T2MLR (Cai et al., 2026) routes a deeper representation from the previous token into an earlier layer through a gated pathway. T2MLR is the closest to our Jacobi refiner, but its recurrent object is a cached vertical representation, whereas our Jacobi refiner links the top and bottom of a lattice of horizontal states that each follow their own temporal recurrence. Recirculation (Mozer et al., 2026b) also sends deep activations to shallower layers across steps, but is a training-free, inference-time intervention with sequential prefill, whereas the Lattice is trained end to end in a token-parallel fashion. The State-Prediction Separation Transformer (Monea et al., 2026) shares our view that a single representation can be burdened by multiple roles, but separates them within each token’s computation rather than keeping a persistent latent at each layer.

A.2 Additional Method Details

A.2.1 Decoding Modulation (How the horizontal latents act)

When this optional head is enabled, the topmost Lattice layer’s horizontal latent, with its own normalization, joins the final vertical latent in a shared readout space of dimension dsd_{s}, and the next token is decoded from their sum:

p⁡(xt+1∣x≤t)=softmax⁡(WU​(Pv​Norm​(htN)+Pr​Normhead​(rttop))),p(x_{t+1}\mid x_{\leq t})=\mathrm{softmax}\Big(W_{U}\big(P_{v}\mathrm{Norm}(h_{t}^{N})+P_{r}\mathrm{Norm}_{\mathrm{head}}(r_{t}^{\mathrm{top}})\big)\Big),

where Pv∈ℝds×dmodelP_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{s}\times d_{\mathrm{model}}} and Pr∈ℝds×drP_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{s}\times d_{r}} are learned projections and WU∈ℝV×dsW_{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d_{s}} maps to vocabulary logits. Like every other injection in Sec. 3.2.1, PrP_{r} is zero-initialized. Hence at initialization the horizontal latent contributes nothing: attention and the MLP reduce to the standard Transformer layer, and the output is decoded from the vertical latent alone. The horizontal latent gains influence only through training. We use decoding modulation only in experiments with a highly compressed vertical latent (dmodel=256d_{\mathrm{model}}{=}256). When enabled, the horizontal decoding head reads the separately normalized raw top-layer state rttopr_{t}^{\mathrm{top}}, not the vstream-enriched readout.

A.2.2 Input Injection (How the horizontal latents are updated)

The base update receives new information only through htℓ−1h_{t}^{\ell-1}, so its access to the current input is limited by what the vertical latent preserves, which we probe by ablating a narrower vertical latent (Fig. 6). By layer ℓ\ell, the vertical latent may also have discarded information about the raw token identity. Input injection (inj) therefore feeds the token embedding, with its own normalized read h^t0=Norme​(ht0)\hat{h}_{t}^{0}=\mathrm{Norm}_{e}(h_{t}^{0}), directly into both pre-activations of the update:

Δtℓ\displaystyle\Delta_{t}^{\ell} =softplus⁡(WΔℓ​ntℓ+We,Δℓ​h^t0+bΔℓ)\displaystyle=\mathrm{softplus}\big(W_{\Delta}^{\ell}n_{t}^{\ell}+W_{e,\Delta}^{\ell}\hat{h}_{t}^{0}+b_{\Delta}^{\ell}\big)
ctℓ\displaystyle c_{t}^{\ell} =SiLU⁡(Wrℓ​ntℓ+We,cℓ​h^t0+brℓ)\displaystyle=\mathrm{SiLU}\big(W_{r}^{\ell}n_{t}^{\ell}+W_{e,c}^{\ell}\hat{h}_{t}^{0}+b_{r}^{\ell}\big)

with We,ΔℓW_{e,\Delta}^{\ell} and We,cℓW_{e,c}^{\ell} zero-initialized. The recurrence rtℓ=gtℓ⊙rt−1ℓ+btℓr_{t}^{\ell}=g_{t}^{\ell}\odot r_{t-1}^{\ell}+b_{t}^{\ell} is otherwise unchanged: Δtℓ\Delta_{t}^{\ell} and ctℓc_{t}^{\ell} still depend only on current-timestep inputs (ntℓn_{t}^{\ell} and h^t0\hat{h}_{t}^{0}), never on rt−1ℓr_{t-1}^{\ell}, so the transition remains exactly affine and the same parallel scan applies.

A.2.3 Jacobi Refiner (How the horizontal latents are updated)

The input-injection and vstream pathways use only information available at the current timestep, so the base update keeps an exact parallel scan across time. Neither feeds a higher layer’s horizontal latent back to a lower layer at the next timestep. Such top-to-bottom feedback is straightforward in a token-by-token rollout, but breaks the single bottom-to-top sweep of teacher-forced training, because the top layer’s latent is not yet available when the bottom layer updates. Following Zeng et al. (2026); Wu et al. (2026), we approximate it during training with Jacobi iteration. Unlike these works, which iterate over a recurrence that feeds the final vertical latent back as the next input, we apply it to the horizontal latents.

Sweeps.

Let J≥1J\geq 1 be the total number of sweeps: J0 denotes the base single pass and J3 a base pass followed by two refinement sweeps. Sweep j=0j=0 runs the Lattice block bottom to top exactly as in the base update, producing rtℓ,(0)r_{t}^{\ell,(0)} for every layer and timestep. Each subsequent sweep j=1,…,J−1j=1,\dots,J-1 takes the top Lattice layer’s latent from the previous sweep, shifted one timestep back, and maps it through a SwiGLU:

Nt(j)\displaystyle N_{t}^{(j)} =WJ,down​(SiLU⁡(WJ,gate​z^t(j−1))⊙(WJ,up​z^t(j−1))),z^t(j−1)=RMSNorm⁡(rt−1top,(j−1)),\displaystyle=W_{J,\mathrm{down}}\big(\mathrm{SiLU}(W_{J,\mathrm{gate}}\hat{z}_{t}^{(j-1)})\odot(W_{J,\mathrm{up}}\hat{z}_{t}^{(j-1)})\big),\qquad\hat{z}_{t}^{(j-1)}=\mathrm{RMSNorm}\big(r_{t-1}^{\mathrm{top},(j-1)}\big),

with hidden width 2​dr2d_{r}, z^\hat{z} set to zero at the first timestep, and Nt(0)=0N_{t}^{(0)}=0. Only the bottom Lattice layer ℓ0\ell_{0} receives the correction, which is added to its candidate content ctℓ0,(j)=SiLU⁡(Wrℓ0​ntℓ0,(j)+brℓ0)c_{t}^{\ell_{0},(j)}=\mathrm{SiLU}(W_{r}^{\ell_{0}}n_{t}^{\ell_{0},(j)}+b_{r}^{\ell_{0}}), computed from the normalized vertical input ntℓ0,(j)n_{t}^{\ell_{0},(j)} (plus the input-injection term when used; full update in Sec. 3.2.2):

btℓ0,(j)=(1−gtℓ0,(j))⊙(ctℓ0,(j)+Nt(j)),\displaystyle b_{t}^{\ell_{0},(j)}=(1-g_{t}^{\ell_{0},(j)})\odot\big(c_{t}^{\ell_{0},(j)}+N_{t}^{(j)}\big),

which enters the same affine recurrence rtℓ=gtℓ⊙rt−1ℓ+btℓr_{t}^{\ell}=g_{t}^{\ell}\odot r_{t-1}^{\ell}+b_{t}^{\ell}. Every sweep reruns the whole Lattice block from the same early-block outputs and the same learned initial states, with parameters shared across sweeps and all layer inputs and coefficients recomputed; the final sweep supplies the block output. Because Nt(j)N_{t}^{(j)} depends only on the fully resolved previous sweep, each sweep’s scan remains exactly affine and token-parallel; the cost is JJ serial sweeps instead of one.

Training and inference.

WJ,gateW_{J,\mathrm{gate}} and WJ,upW_{J,\mathrm{up}} are initialized from 𝒩⁡(0,0.022)\mathcal{N}(0,0.02^{2}) and WJ,downW_{J,\mathrm{down}} is zero-initialized, so a J3 model equals its J0 counterpart at initialization. We train with a fixed number of sweeps (J=3J=3) and backpropagate through all of them. At inference, the top-layer latent of the preceding token is already available, so exact recurrence (Nt=F⁡(rt−1top)N_{t}=F(r_{t-1}^{\mathrm{top}})) can be evaluated in a single token-by-token pass without refinement sweeps (“sequential rollout”); finite number of sweeps need not reproduce this rollout. We report both three-sweep & sequential-rollout eval (Sec. 4.1).

A.3 Additional Experimental Results

A.3.1 Transformer Backbones

Scaling to 30B tokens.

Building on the 20B-token results in Table 1, Table 3 shows that the benefits of the Lattice persist under substantially longer, post-Chinchilla pretraining on 30B tokens. At the matched 400M scale, LLLM(908,256)(908,256) with input-injection + vstream outperforms Base-24L on every reported metric, reducing FineWeb-Edu, Pile, LAMBADA-OpenAI, and LAMBADA-Standard perplexity by 5.4%5.4\%, 8.9%8.9\%, 8.1%8.1\%, and 11.2%11.2\%, respectively, while improving the two LAMBADA accuracies by 2.902.90 and 3.403.40 points. The gains also hold at 600M parameters: LLLM(1024,1024)(1024,1024) improves over the similarly sized Base-40L by 4.4%4.4\% on FineWeb-Edu, 4.6%4.6\% on LAMBADA-OpenAI, and 7.3%7.3\% on LAMBADA-Standard, while increasing their accuracies by 1.791.79 and 0.750.75 points; Base-40L remains modestly better on Pile. Thus, the advantages observed at 20B tokens do not disappear with extended pretraining. Moreover, the strong results obtained with different vertical–horizontal allocations suggest that this capacity split is an important tuning axis, and that a more systematic search may yield further improvements.

Downstream task performance.

Table 4 breaks down the nine-task averages of Sec. 4.1 by task after 20B-token pretraining. At the matched 400M scale, LLLM(945,256)(945,256) J3 improves on Base-24L on all nine tasks in both the zero- and five-shot settings. At 600M, LLLM(1024,1024)(1024,1024) improves on Base-40L on all nine tasks five-shot and on eight of nine zero-shot, trailing only on WinoGrande (52.452.4 vs. 53.353.3). LLLM(512,512)(512,512) with 40 layers also exceeds the 609M Base-40L in both settings (48.1048.10 vs. 47.3647.36 zero-shot; 48.5048.50 vs. 47.3747.37 five-shot) with 495M parameters.

Top-to-bottom Residual Stream Refinement Ablations.

Fig. 9 tests whether top-to-bottom feedback across timesteps helps the vertical residual stream, the horizontal latents, or both. All models are trained on 10B FineWeb-Edu tokens with the Transformer recipe (App. A.4.1); Lattice models use the vstream-only configuration (dmodel=932d_{\mathrm{model}}{=}932, dr=256d_{r}{=}256). Jacobi on vertical passes the previous token’s final-layer state through a small MLP and adds it to the next token’s embedding, similar to the Full-Bandwidth Transformer (Wang et al., 2026). Jacobi on Lattice applies the Jacobi refiner (App. A.2.3) to the horizontal latents, and the last variant applies both. All three are trained and evaluated with three parallel, teacher-forced sweeps (J3). Vertical feedback lowers the Transformer’s perplexity from 16.9416.94 to 15.3615.36 (−9.3%-9.3\%), slightly below the single-pass Lattice (15.5215.52), but it reruns the full network three times and adds 6.36.3 M parameters. Feedback on horizontal latents lowers the Lattice from 15.5215.52 to 15.0915.09 (−2.8%-2.8\%). Combining both works the best, 14.9214.92 (−3.9%-3.9\% relative to single-pass Lattice), so two forms of feedback are complementary.

Stateless vs. Lattice modulation.

Is the gain of the Lattice due to its recurrent history, or would any extra input-dependent FiLM conditioning suffice? Fig. 10 replaces the horizontal latent r^tℓ\hat{r}_{t}^{\ell} with a stateless signal ztℓ=Norm⁡(Pℓ​Norm​(ut))∈ℝ256z_{t}^{\ell}=\mathrm{Norm}\big(P^{\ell}\,\mathrm{Norm}(u_{t})\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{256}, where PℓP^{\ell} is a learned per-layer projection and utu_{t} is either the layer’s incoming residual stream htℓ−1h_{t}^{\ell-1} (residual-stream-conditioned) or the token embedding ht0h_{t}^{0} (input-conditioned). We then perform FiLM based QKV and/or MLP modulation with this signal. Everything else matches the Lattice: the same E1/L20/D1 split, the same zero-initialized FiLM heads on QKV (and optionally the MLP), and widths adjusted so that all models have ∼\sim406 M parameters; only the recurrence across timesteps is removed. All models are trained on 10B FineWeb-Edu tokens with the Transformer recipe (App. A.4.1). Stateless modulation helps: input-conditioned QKV modulation lowers the Transformer’s perplexity from 16.9416.94 to 16.2916.29 (−3.8%-3.8\%), and conditioning on the raw embedding beats conditioning on the residual stream (16.6216.62), consistent with input injection helping the horizontal update. Recurrent conditioning helps more at matched parameters: with QKV modulation alone the Lattice reaches 15.9915.99 (−1.9%-1.9\% vs. the best stateless variant), and with QKV+MLP modulation 15.6315.63 (−4.2%-4.2\% vs. 16.3216.32), improving to 15.4915.49 with inj+vs. MLP modulation also helps only when the conditioning carries history: it slightly hurts both stateless variants but improves the Lattice from 15.9915.99 to 15.6315.63. These results are consistent with the hypothesis that the history accumulated in the horizontal latents, rather than extra conditioning capacity alone, drives most of the Lattice’s gain.

Lattice vs. short convolutions.

Short causal convolutions on the attention inputs let local context shape q,k,vq,k,v, similar in spirit to how the Lattice conditions attention on history. Static short convolutions, such as Canon layers (Allen-Zhu, 2026), mix each token’s representation with those of its few preceding tokens using learned, input-independent filters; dynamic short convolutions (Sieberling et al., 2026) instead generate the filter weights from the input. Fig. 11 compares them after 10B-token pretraining. A width-4 static depthwise convolution on q,k,vq,k,v adds only 0.280.28 M parameters to the Transformer and lowers perplexity from 16.9416.94 to 15.8715.87 (−6.3%-6.3\%); a width-4 dynamic convolution reaches 15.5215.52 with 5.85.8 M extra parameters. The Lattice matches dynamic convolution (15.4915.49) with 6.86.8 M fewer parameters, and the two are complementary: adding dynamic convolution to the Lattice lowers perplexity to 14.9914.99 (−3.4%-3.4\% vs. dynamic convolution alone). A convolution, static or dynamic, aggregates only a fixed window of recent tokens, whereas the horizontal latents carry history across the whole sequence through their recurrence, thus advances in parallelizable nonlinear updates could strengthen the Lattice further.

GSM8K-Aug finetuning.

We finetune each 20B-token checkpoint on GSM8K-Aug (385,620385{,}620 problems), following the chain-of-thought (CoT) stage of Coconut (Hao et al., 2024): conditioned on the question, the model is trained with the next-token loss on the intermediate equation steps and the final answer, with question tokens masked from the loss. We sweep the learning rate separately for each model over {10−4,4×10−4,8×10−4}\{10^{-4},4\times 10^{-4},8\times 10^{-4}\}; 8×10−48\times 10^{-4} performs best for every model. All other settings are shared: AdamW with a learning rate that is constant after a linear warmup over the first 3%3\% of steps, wd 0.010.01, gradient clipping at 1.01.0, batch size 128128, bf16, and 44 epochs (1212K steps), with one run (seed 00) per model. J3 models use 3 Jacobi sweeps in both finetuning & decoding.

We report accuracy on the GSM8K test set (1,3191{,}319 problems) and, without further training, on GSM-Hard (1,3191{,}319), MultiArith (600600), ASDiv (2,3052{,}305), and a 1,0001{,}000-problem SVAMP subset (SVAMP-1K). Table 5 evaluates how well the 20B-token-pretrained models transfer after finetuning on GSM8K-Aug. At the 400M scale, every LLLM variant outperforms the matched Base-24L Transformer across all five reasoning benchmarks.

LLLM(945,256)(945,256) J3 achieves the highest mean accuracy, improving from 36.0236.02 to 48.1048.10 (+12.08+12.08 points), and obtains the strongest GSM8K and SVAMP-1K results. The base-update model performs best on MultiArith and GSM-Hard, while input injection and vstream produce the best ASDiv accuracy; these differences among Lattice variants are small (at most 3.23.2 points). The trend persists at the 600M scale: LLLM(1024,1024)(1024,1024) outperforms the 609M Base-40L Transformer on every task and raises mean accuracy from 40.2440.24 to 47.7447.74 (+7.50+7.50 points), despite using slightly fewer parameters. These results show that gains from horizontal latent capacity transfer beyond pretraining perplexity to math reasoning. Finetuned accuracy is not determined by pretraining quality alone: Base-40L and LLLM(908,256)(908,256) with input-injection + vstream have the same FineWeb-Edu perplexity (14.4014.40) and nearly the same zero-shot average (47.3647.36 vs. 47.3847.38), yet differ by 10.110.1 points on GSM8K (33.533.5 vs. 43.643.6). Since each model is finetuned once, we do not interpret the small differences among Lattice variants; the gap to the Transformers is larger and consistent, with every Lattice model ahead of every Transformer baseline by at least 10.110.1 GSM8K points at both scales.

A.3.2 Recurrent Backbones

Downstream evaluation.

Figs. 12 and 13 show the per-state-budget nine-task averages summarized in Sec. 4.3. At each state budget and shot setting, the Lattice point is the best of input-injection + vstream and two vstream-only variants that reduce either dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}} or the FFN width; all variants are within 0.1%0.1\% of the pure model’s parameter count. Because this selection is post hoc, the gains should be read as those of the best coupling rather than of a single preselected one. The Lattice model is ahead in 29 of 30 pairs; the only regression is the hybrid at 128K in the five-shot setting (45.02→44.8045.02\rightarrow 44.80).

A.3.3 Residual Streams

Learned value residuals.

The fixed value residual of Fig. 3 mixes the first-layer and current values with constant weights of 0.50.5; here we learn these weights (App. A.4.2). Fig. 14 reports validation FineWeb-Edu perplexity after 20B tokens. Learning the weights improves on the fixed mix, e.g., Transformer + value 14.69→14.5814.69\to 14.58, Lattice + value 14.26→14.1314.26\to 14.13. Across all four configurations of Fig. 14, the Lattice lowers perplexity by 3.03.0–7.0%7.0\%. On top of HC + x0, however, learned value residuals add little: −0.3%-0.3\% for the Transformer (14.22→14.1814.22\to 14.18) and none for the Lattice (13.61→13.6213.61\to 13.62). Lattice + HC + x0 therefore remains the best model overall.

A.4 Training Details

Unless otherwise noted, all models use the same training recipe; only model width and depth, token budget, and Lattice-specific settings vary across runs.

A.4.1 Transformer Backbones

Backbone.

We build on a LLaMA-style decoder with the GPT-NeoX tokenizer (vocabulary size V=50,304V=50{,}304). Layers use pre-RMSNorm (ϵ=10−5\epsilon=10^{-5}), rotary position embeddings (RoPE) with a context length of 20482048, SwiGLU MLPs with intermediate size 27522752, and an untied output head. Attention uses 1616 query heads and 1616 key/value heads, each of dimension 6464, so the attention width (16×64=102416\times 64=1024) is fixed and decoupled from the residual-stream (vertical-latent) width dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}}. We vary dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}}∈{256,512,908,932,945,1024,…}\in\{256,512,908,932,945,1024,\dots\} and the depth N∈{22,24,40}N\in\{22,24,40\} to sweep model size. Input embeddings are scaled by dmodel\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{model}}}. Backbone attention and MLP projections have no biases, and all weights not listed below use the standard 𝒩⁡(0,0.022)\mathcal{N}(0,0.02^{2}) initialization.

Optimizer.

We use AdamW with β1=0.9\beta_{1}{=}0.9, β2=0.95\beta_{2}{=}0.95, weight decay 0.10.1, and gradient-norm clipping at 1.01.0. Weight decay is not applied to biases, to the gains of the backbone RMSNorm layers, or, following Mamba-2 practice, to the horizontal-latent decay parameters A​_​log\mathrm{A\_log} and dt​_​bias\mathrm{dt\_bias}; all other parameters, including the learned initial state r0r_{0} and the normalization gains inside the Lattice update, are decayed. All Lattice injection maps—the FiLM γ/β\gamma/\beta projections, input-injection and vstream maps, Jacobi refiner’s output projection, and output-head carry projection—are zero-initialized. Consequently, the Lattice model is functionally identical to a plain Transformer of the same width and depth at initialization, and the horizontal latent acquires influence only through training.

Learning-rate schedule.

The peak learning rate is 1×10−31\times 10^{-3} and is decayed with a cosine schedule to a floor of 10%10\% of the peak (cosine_with_min_lr, min_lr_rate=0.1\texttt{min\_lr\_rate}{=}0.1), following a linear warmup over the first 2%2\% of training steps. We tuned the peak learning rate by grid search for both the Transformer and Lattice backbones.

Batching and schedule length.

We use a global batch size of 512512 sequences of length 20482048 (≈1.05\approx 1.05M tokens per step), realized with a per-device batch size of 88 and gradient accumulation of 88 across 88 GPUs. Token budgets correspond to 9,5379{,}537 steps for 10B tokens, 19,07419{,}074 for 20B, and 28,61128{,}611 for 30B.

Precision and kernels.

Training uses bfloat16 mixed precision, FlashAttention-2, and gradient checkpointing; attention inside Lattice layers uses PyTorch’s fused scaled-dot-product attention. For numerical stability, the diagonal gated-linear carry scan and its FiLM application are computed in fp32.

Data.

We pretrain on FineWeb-Edu, pre-tokenized with the NeoX tokenizer and packed into contiguous 20482048-token sequences (10B-, 20B-, and 30B-token subsets). Perplexity is reported on a deduplicated, contamination-checked, held-out FineWeb-Edu split, and out-of-domain perplexity on Pile, LAMBADA, and Nemotron-CC (Sec. 4.1).

Lattice configuration.

An LLLM is specified by its early/Lattice/late split E/L/DE/L/D (e.g., E​1/L​20/D​1E1/L20/D1 or E​4/L​16/D​4E4/L16/D4, with horizontal latents only in the LL block), the horizontal-latent width drd_{r} (256256 for the 400M models; dr=dmodeld_{r}{=}d_{\mathrm{model}} for LLLM(512,512)(512,512) and LLLM(1024,1024)(1024,1024)), groupwise FiLM in which each attention head shares its multiplicative gain (γ\gamma) across 44 channel groups, and the number of Jacobi sweeps J∈{0,3}J\in\{0,3\}.

A.4.2 Residual-Stream Enhancements

Setup.

Fig. 3 (Sec. 4.2) compares ten 400M models trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens (19,07419{,}074 steps) with the Transformer recipe above, changing only the residual stream. The seven Transformer variants (plain, +HC, +mHC, +value, +x0, +HC + x0, +x0 + value) use the 24-layer, dmodel=1024d_{\mathrm{model}}{=}1024 model. The three Lattice variants (+Lattice, +Lattice + HC, +Lattice + HC + x0) use the vstream-only configuration (E1/L20/D1, dmodel=932d_{\mathrm{model}}{=}932, dr=256d_{r}{=}256, no input injection), narrowed to stay iso-parameter with the Transformer. Fig. 14 (App. A.3.3) adds four runs with learned value residuals, two Transformers and their Lattice counterparts.

Input residual (x0).

Following nanochat (Karpathy, 2025), we compute h0=RMSNorm⁡(scaled token embedding)h^{0}=\mathrm{RMSNorm}(\text{scaled token embedding}) once, without a learned gain, and before every layer ℓ\ell (early, Lattice, and late) set h←λrℓ​h+λ0ℓ​h0h\leftarrow\lambda_{r}^{\ell}h+\lambda_{0}^{\ell}h^{0}. The 2​N2N scalars are initialized linearly in depth, λ0ℓ=0.20−0.15​ℓ/(N−1)\lambda_{0}^{\ell}=0.20-0.15\,\ell/(N{-}1) and λrℓ=1.15−0.10​ℓ/(N−1)\lambda_{r}^{\ell}=1.15-0.10\,\ell/(N{-}1), and trained in separate AdamW groups: λ0\lambda_{0} at 25×25\times the base learning rate (2.5×10−22.5\times 10^{-2}) without weight decay, and λr\lambda_{r} at 0.25×0.25\times (2.5×10−42.5\times 10^{-4}) with weight decay 0.050.05; both follow the same warmup and cosine schedule.

Value residual.

In Fig. 3, we use the fixed (constant) ResFormer variant (Zhou et al., 2025): every layer after the first replaces its values with 12​v1+12​vℓ\tfrac{1}{2}v^{1}+\tfrac{1}{2}v^{\ell}, with no added parameters. The learned variant (all results in Fig. 14) instead uses αℓ​v1+βℓ​vℓ\alpha^{\ell}v^{1}+\beta^{\ell}v^{\ell}, with two unconstrained scalars per layer initialized to 0.50.5, adding 2​(N−1)2(N{-}1) parameters (4646 for the Transformer, 4242 for the Lattice). Like the x0 scalars, αℓ\alpha^{\ell} is trained at 25×25\times the base learning rate without weight decay, and βℓ\beta^{\ell} at 0.25×0.25\times with decay 0.050.05.

Hyper-connections.

HC (Zhu et al., 2025) and mHC (Xie et al., 2026) use n=4n{=}4 residual streams, each initialized with a copy of the token embedding and summed before the final RMSNorm. Each attention and MLP sub-layer has its own router with three sets of weights: read weights that mix the nn streams into the sub-layer input, write weights that distribute the sub-layer output back to the streams, and an n×nn\times n mixing matrix that recombines the streams. In HC, following the dynamic formulation of Zhu et al. (2025) (App. J), each weight is a static term plus a token-dependent term computed from the LayerNorm-normalized streams. The static terms are initialized so that each sub-layer reads from one stream and the mixing matrix is the identity; the token-dependent terms are zero-initialized and scaled by learnable gates initialized to 0.010.01. The attention and MLP output projections are scaled by 1/n=0.51/\sqrt{n}=0.5 at initialization. In mHC, following Xie et al. (2026) (Eqs. 7–9), a single linear map of the RMS-normalized, flattened streams produces all three: read weights σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot), write weights 2​σ​(⋅)2\sigma(\cdot), and mixing logits, which 2020 Sinkhorn–Knopp iterations project toward a doubly stochastic matrix. The static biases are zero for the read and write weights and the identity for the mixing logits. In both, the static router weights are excluded from weight decay.

Composition with the Lattice.

We combine the Lattice with HC: each Lattice layer keeps a single horizontal latent, shared by all four streams, which reads the attention router’s mixed input and steers the attention and MLP exactly as in the single-stream model. The horizontal latent does not modulate the HC read, write, or mixing weights; we leave this to future work. Parameter counts are 406.65406.65 M (Transformer), 407.03407.03 M (HC), 411.36411.36 M (mHC), 405.52405.52 M (Lattice), and 405.85405.85 M (Lattice + HC); x0 adds only 2​N2N scalars, the fixed value residual none, and the learned value residual 2​(N−1)2(N{-}1).

A.4.3 Recurrent Backbones

Common setup.

All recurrent models (Sec. 4.3) are attention-free stacks of 2222 pre-RMSNorm layers, each a token mixer followed by a SwiGLU MLP (intermediate size 27522752), with the GPT-NeoX vocabulary (V=50,304V=50{,}304), untied embeddings, and no positional encoding. All mixers run on the Triton kernels of the flash-linear-attention library (fla, v0.4.1)22 2 github.com/fla-org/flash-linear-attention; we add only a small PyTorch-2.4 compatibility shim and modify no kernel or layer code.. Baseline and Lattice models share the same mixer code; the Lattice versions only add the steering described below. Native-state geometries and widths are listed in Tab. 7.

GDN.

We use fla’s GatedDeltaNet layer (Yang et al., 2025) unchanged: short causal convolutions on q,k,vq,k,v, in-kernel L2L_{2} normalization of qq and kk, per-head decay α\alpha and write strength β\beta, a gated output RMSNorm, and the chunked training kernel. The state per head is dk×dvd_{k}\times d_{v}, varied through the number of heads HH and the per-head key and value dimensions.

Mamba2.

We implement the Mamba-2 SSD layer (Dao and Gu, 2024) on fla’s chunk_simple_gla kernel rather than the mamba_ssm package: a joint input projection to [z,x​B​C,Δ][z,\,xBC,\,\Delta], a size-4 depthwise causal convolution with SiLU on x​B​CxBC, a scalar per-head decay Δ​A\Delta A with A=−exp⁡(Alog)A=-\exp(A_{\log}) and AlogA_{\log} initialized to log⁡(1,…,H)\log(1,\dots,H), values x​Δx\Delta, a DD skip connection, a zz-gated RMSNorm, and the standard log-uniform Δ\Delta-bias initialization on [10−3,10−1][10^{-3},10^{-1}]. The inner width is H⋅dhead=1024H\cdot d_{\mathrm{head}}=1024 with one B/CB/C group, and the state per head is dstate×dheadd_{\mathrm{state}}\times d_{\mathrm{head}}.

Triadic GDN.

The official triadic linear attention kernels support only a per-head key dimension of 128128 on Hopper/Blackwell GPUs and provide no fallback, so we reimplement the layer inside our GDN stack. Each head writes with the joint key κ=k2⊗k\kappa=k_{2}\otimes k and reads with the joint query π=q2⊗q\pi=q_{2}\otimes q, where k,q∈ℝdkk,q\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}} are L2L_{2}-normalized GDN-style factors and k2,q2∈ℝEk_{2},q_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{E} (E=2E{=}2 slices) are L2L_{2}-normalized softplus projections of the input. The recurrence is the standard gated delta rule on the joint key dimension E​dkEd_{k}, computed with fla’s chunk_gated_delta_rule. Our one simplification relative to the original is a scalar per-head decay shared across slices.

GDN–Mamba2 hybrid.

We follow the Gated DeltaNet-H2 layout (Yang et al., 2025) with only GDN and Mamba layers: 1111 blocks of [Mamba2, MLP, GDN, MLP], i.e., 2222 mixers. Its Mamba2 and GDN layers are the same as in the pure backbones above.

Adding the Lattice.

Each Lattice layer adds the same horizontal-latent update as in the Transformer, with dr=256d_{r}=256, input injection, and vstream. The pure GDN, Mamba2, and Triadic GDN backbones use E1/L20/D1, so 2020 of the 2222 mixer layers carry a latent. The hybrid applies the same split at the level of its 1111 blocks (E1/L9/D1): each of the 99 Lattice blocks gives its Mamba2 mixer and its GDN mixer their own latent, for 1818 latents in total. Instead of attention, the latent steers the mixer by FiLM, x←x⊙(1+tanh⁡γ)+βx\leftarrow x\odot(1+\tanh\gamma)+\beta, applied to every quantity that controls native-memory writes and reads: for GDN, q,k,vq,k,v (after the short convolution and before L2L_{2} normalization), the decay and write-strength logits (before softplus and sigmoid), and the output-gate input; for Mamba2, CC, BB, xx (the analogues of q,k,vq,k,v), the per-head Δ\Delta logit (before softplus), and zz; for Triadic GDN, additionally the k2,q2k_{2},q_{2} logits before softplus. The MLPs, the output head, and the native-state geometry are unchanged, and all FiLM maps are zero-initialized, so each Lattice model equals its pure counterpart of the same width at initialization. To keep each pair iso-parameter, we reduce dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}} of the Lattice model (Tab. 7). The two vstream-only variants used for downstream selection have no input injection and instead either reduce dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}} at FFN width 27522752 or keep dmodel=1024d_{\mathrm{model}}{=}1024 and reduce the FFN width.

Training.

All recurrent runs use a standalone PyTorch DDP trainer on 88 GPUs with the Transformer recipe above (AdamW, peak learning rate 10−310^{-3}, cosine decay to 10%10\%, weight decay 0.10.1, clipping 1.01.0, global batch 512×2048512\times 2048, 9,5379{,}537 steps ≈\approx 10B FineWeb-Edu tokens, bfloat16, gradient checkpointing, seed 4242), with two differences: linear warmup over the first 10%10\% of steps, and weight decay applied only to matrices other than the token embedding (no decay on embeddings, normalization gains, biases, r0r_{0}, AlogA_{\log}, Δ\Delta/dt biases, or DD). Pure and Lattice models within each pair share this recipe exactly.
